summary:
Van is a province of Turkey and stands under the national framework: the country's penal code, migration rules, health regulations and prison administration apply here in full, and no trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation exists for Van itself. That absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence, not local permissiveness.

A leaked omnibus measure identified by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 as the "11th Judicial Package" would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, conditioned on mandatory permanent infertility assessment and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years, patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warned it would drive treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest. As reported, the draft had not been passed; its pending status has not prevented authorities elsewhere from acting as though equivalent prohibitions were already in force.

Kaos GL's 2025 review characterises hostility as explicit state policy rather than residual prejudice: "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions, the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation for the first time in years, restricted expression and artistic freedom, and events cancelled or banned. The monitoring counted 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected; 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the previous year; 313 liberty violations, roughly two and a half times the prior year, carrying 299 detention decisions; private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy; and 61 travel bans.

For a visitor, the most likely contact with this machinery is a street checkpoint. Turkish authorities require foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release, an practice legal experts cited in the reporting argue violates Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One woman stopped stated that no fines were issued but that she was documented anyway, and that enforcement was already being applied ahead of any new law. Every such interaction is an occasion on which documents are compared against presentation, and any mismatch between passport gender marker and appearance is an outing risk.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required electronic reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care; anyone relying on hormone therapy in transit should expect records to carry a gender marker consequence.
tangentialFactors:
Prison conditions are a live risk for any trans visitor detained in Turkey. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Coordinated by Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın, rights groups demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to registered sex, with a trans man held in a women's prison, and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

The pattern has depth. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's continuity rather than as a statement of current law.
localsOnly:
Residents of Van live under the national policy direction described in Kaos GL's 2025 review: "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions, expression and artistic freedom restricted, events cancelled or banned, and the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation for the first time in years.

Residents face 61 travel bans recorded nationally in 2025 and private-life violations that rose from 16 to 67, including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy. Residents have been affected by 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the prior year, and 299 detention decisions under 313 liberty violations.

The September 2025 Health Ministry regulation and the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that preceded it govern resident access to transition care directly: hospitals may no longer record the "other" option and must issue electronic reports, adding "gender reassignment" as an official medical-board reason, which places transition-related care into identifiable official records.

Residents placed in custody are assigned by registered sex. The Poyraz case and the parliamentary question of 12 December 2025 confirmed that a trans man had been held in a women's prison, and that the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and ILGA World-sourced documentation of isolation, strip searches and ineffective complaints describes the conditions residents, rather than visitors, enter.

Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft judicial package, and civic groups protested it, so domestic advocacy channels exist even as the measure remains pending.
outOfScopeNotes:
Neither Human Rights Watch's October 2025 release nor Kaos GL's 2025 review provides a provincial breakdown, so the counts cited here are national totals and cannot be attributed to Van. No Van-specific incident, arrest, protest or police practice is sourced in this inventory; that gap is unresolved rather than evidence that no such events occurred.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted remains unresolved: Human Rights Watch reported it as a leaked draft before the government as of 29 October 2025 and warned of its effects, but the inventory contains no later legislative record confirming or denying passage.

No source states whether health directorates in Van issued circulars parallel to the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate's, or which hospitals in the province are designated for medical-board evaluations. Local policing practice at Van's checkpoints, including whether GBT-style stops of trans people occur here, is not documented in this inventory.

The 2008 Human Rights Watch report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is not a statement of current law.
